Ability means the power to do something. It is the answer to the question: "Can this person actually do this thing?"

When someone has the ability to do something, it means they possess what it takes — the mental power, the physical capacity, the skill, or the knowledge — to actually carry it out.

A bird has the ability to fly. A fish does not.
She has the ability to solve complex math problems.
He lost the ability to walk after his accident.

Notice that "ability" is about what is possible for someone — what lies within their reach.

Ability can come from two sources, and this matters:

1. Natural ability — something you are born with. Some people are naturally gifted at music, athletics, or learning languages. They didn't earn it through hard work; they simply have it. This is sometimes called a natural talent, but the word "ability" covers it perfectly.

She showed a natural ability for drawing even as a child.

2. Acquired (or developed) ability — something you gain through practice, education, or experience. Most abilities in life fall here. You weren't born knowing how to drive a car or write code — you learned it, and now you can do it.

After years of training, he had the ability to speak four languages.

In everyday use, "ability" covers both kinds without needing to specify which one, unless you want to.

Having the "ability" to do something doesn't mean doing it perfectly. It simply means you can do it — but the level at which you can do it varies widely.

Think of it as a scale:

  • At the low end: You barely manage it. You can do it, but with difficulty.
  • In the middle: You do it competently and reliably.
  • At the high end: You do it with exceptional skill and ease.

This is why you'll often see ability described with words like great, limited, remarkable, poor, or extraordinary — because ability comes in degrees.

He has limited ability in swimming — he can stay afloat, but only just.
She has remarkable ability as a surgeon.
Ability Can Be General or Specific

General ability refers to broad mental or physical capacity — the overall potential a person has.

He is a person of great ability. (meaning: he is broadly capable and intelligent)

Specific ability refers to being able to do one particular thing.

She has the ability to memorize long texts quickly.
The machine has the ability to process 10,000 records per second.

Both uses are equally correct. Context makes clear which one is meant.

These words are close cousins, but each has a slightly different shade of meaning:

Skill — Skill is always something learned and practiced. It implies that you have refined a specific ability through deliberate effort and repetition. All skills are abilities, but not all abilities are skills.

Playing the piano is a skill. (It had to be learned.)
A child's natural ability to absorb language is not yet a skill.

Talent — Talent specifically refers to a natural, inborn ability. It implies something you were gifted with, not something you worked hard to get. "Ability" is the broader, more neutral word; "talent" emphasizes the natural origin.

She has a talent for music. (She was born with it.)
She has the ability to play the violin. (This is what she can do — however she got there.)

Capability — Very close to ability, but capability often suggests the outer limit of what someone could do under the right conditions. It leans toward potential.

The engine has the capability to reach 200 mph. (Under the right conditions, it can.)
Ability tends to describe what someone actually does or regularly can do, while capability often speaks to what they could do if pushed.

Capacity — Capacity usually refers to the maximum amount something can hold or handle, or the potential to develop a skill or quality. It often sounds more abstract or physiological.

The human brain has a remarkable capacity for learning.
Ability is more about concrete, actual doing; capacity is more about room or potential.

The short rule: when in doubt, use ability — it is the most versatile of all these words.

Here are the most natural ways "ability" is used in sentences, all of which you will encounter repeatedly:

  • "the ability to [do something]" — the most standard structure.

He has the ability to remain calm under pressure.

  • "to the best of one's ability" — meaning as well as one possibly can, using every bit of what they have.

She completed the task to the best of her ability.

  • "of great/limited/exceptional ability" — describing how able someone is overall.

He is a student of great ability.

  • "natural ability" — something one was born with.

Her natural ability made her stand out immediately.

  • "mixed abilities" — used in education to describe groups where learners have different levels of competence.

The teacher was skilled at handling mixed-ability classrooms.

  • "mental/physical/intellectual ability" — specifying what type of ability is being discussed.

The test was designed to measure mental ability.
One Important Distinction: Ability vs. Opportunity

"Ability" is only about what a person can do — their internal power. It says nothing about whether they are allowed to do it or get the chance to do it.

She has the ability to lead a team, but her company never gave her the opportunity.

This is a meaningful distinction in life: a person may have great ability but lack access, opportunity, or permission. "Ability" only covers their side of the equation.
Ability is the power or capacity — whether natural or learned — that a person or thing has to perform an action or achieve a result, and it comes in varying degrees from very little to exceptional.

"Abject" means something bad has reached its absolute lowest, most complete, and most hopeless extreme — with all dignity stripped away.

Think of it as a word that doesn't just say "this is bad." It says "this is as bad as it can possibly be — total, crushing, and without a single redeeming quality."

It is always, without exception, used with negative things. You would never say "abject happiness" or "abject success." The word lives permanently in the territory of the dark and the degrading.
The Two Ways It Is Used

"Abject" has two related uses. Once you understand both, you will feel completely at home with this word.

1. To describe a terrible condition or state

Here, "abject" tells you that a bad situation is not mild or partial — it is total and devastating.

  • Abject poverty is not just being poor. It is the most extreme, crushing kind of poverty imaginable — no food, no shelter, no hope, and no dignity. The very worst poverty that exists.
  • Abject failure is not a minor setback. It is a complete and humiliating failure where nothing at all was saved or achieved.
  • Abject misery is not just feeling sad. It is an all-consuming, deep misery from which there seems to be no escape.
  • Abject terror is not feeling nervous. It is total, paralysing fear.

In all of these, "abject" is doing heavy lifting. It tells you: push your mental image of this bad thing to its furthest, lowest, most hopeless extreme — that is what we are talking about.

2. To describe groveling, self-debasing behavior or attitude

This is the second use, and it is equally important. When "abject" describes how a person is behaving or what attitude they are showing, it means they have completely surrendered their self-respect and dignity. They are not just humble — they are prostrating themselves, as if they are nothing.

  • An abject apology is not a simple "I'm sorry." It is an apology so extreme, so groveling, so stripped of any pride that the person seems to be begging for forgiveness on their knees, with zero dignity remaining.
  • Abject submission means giving in entirely and humiliatingly — surrendering all will and resistance.
  • Abject cowardice is not mild nervousness. It is the most complete, shameless display of cowardice, with no courage whatsoever.
The Single Thread That Connects Both Uses

Both uses share one soul: total loss of dignity at the lowest possible extreme.

Whether it describes a condition (abject poverty) or a behavior (an abject apology), "abject" is always pointing to something that has hit absolute rock bottom — something complete, thorough, and utterly without redemption or rescue. That is the throughline.

Words like complete, total, and utter are also intensifiers, but they are neutral — they work with both good and bad things. You can say "a complete success" or "utter joy." You can never do that with "abject."

More importantly, "abject" carries an extra layer that those other words do not: degradation and loss of dignity. So "abject failure" is not just "complete failure" — it is a failure so crushing that there is something humiliating about it. "Abject poverty" is not just "extreme poverty" — it is poverty that has stripped a person of all dignity and humanity.

This is why writers and speakers choose "abject" deliberately. It is not just a stronger "very." It adds the specific flavour of hopelessness, degradation, and the lowest of the low.
Common Words You Will See Paired With "Abject"

These are the most natural and widely used combinations in real life:

  • Abject poverty
  • Abject failure
  • Abject misery
  • Abject terror / fear
  • Abject despair
  • Abject humiliation
  • Abject apology
  • Abject submission / surrender
  • Abject cowardice

Whenever you encounter the word in reading or conversation, it will almost always be paired with one of these or something very similar in spirit.
The One Rule to Never Forget

"Abject" only travels with the negative. If you are ever tempted to pair it with something positive or neutral, stop — the word simply does not go there. Its entire identity is built around the idea of the lowest, most degraded, most hopeless state of something bad.
Abject = the worst, most complete, most degrading extreme of something already bad — with all dignity and hope removed.
82: An abjuration is a formal, solemn, and often public declaration in which a person officially and completely rejects or gives up something they previously believed in, belonged to, or were loyal to — typically under oath.
What makes abjuration different from simply "changing your mind"

If you used to enjoy a TV show and now you don't, that's just a change of taste. No big deal. Abjuration is something far heavier and more deliberate. It is not a quiet, private shift of opinion. It is an announced act — an official declaration made before witnesses, a court, a religious authority, or a governing body. Think of it as signing a binding statement that says: "I hereby formally and permanently reject this."

Three qualities define it. First, it is formal — there is a ceremonial, institutional quality to it; someone in authority is witnessing it. Second, it commonly involves an oath — the person swears (often on a holy text, or before God, or before a court) that they are genuinely and truly abandoning whatever is being renounced. This oath is what gives abjuration its teeth. Third, it is permanent and total — it is not a pause or a hesitation. It is a clean, final severance. The person is declaring they are done, forever.
What kinds of things can be abjured?

Almost anything a person held with deep enough significance that a formal rejection of it carries real weight.

The most classic use historically is the abjuration of a religious belief. During the Middle Ages and the era of the Inquisition, people accused of heresy (beliefs the Church considered false or dangerous) were sometimes forced to make an abjuration — publicly denouncing their "wrong" beliefs and swearing to return to accepted doctrine.

Abjuration also applies to political allegiance. Governments have historically used "Oaths of Abjuration," which were formal documents requiring citizens or subjects to swear they rejected the authority of a particular rival ruler or enemy. Signing such an oath was an act of abjuration — you were cutting your loyalty officially and on the record.

It also applies to a claim to a throne — a king or prince forced to give up his claim to rule would make a formal abjuration of that claim. And in legal contexts, it can apply to citizenship, where renouncing one's nationality before an official body carries the spirit of abjuration.

In short: abjuration is reserved for things that matter — beliefs, loyalties, powers, and identities that carry enough weight that walking away from them requires a solemn public act.

In 1633, the astronomer Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Inquisition for supporting the idea that the Earth revolves around the Sun. Faced with the threat of severe punishment, he made a formal abjuration — publicly and officially declaring that he rejected his own scientific findings and accepted the Church's position instead. It was a coerced, agonizing act of official renunciation. A legend (likely invented, but beautifully fitting) says that after kneeling and making his abjuration, he whispered, "And yet it moves."

This example captures everything abjuration is: weighty, official, public, and often tied to an agonizing conflict between inner conviction and external pressure.

Abjuration is never trivial. What is being abandoned is almost always something the person once held with genuine conviction — a faith, a cause, a loyalty. This is exactly why the word appears so often in stories of persecution, coercion, and moral crisis. It places a person at a crossroads: do I stand by what I truly believe, or do I officially declare I don't believe it to survive?

An abjuration made under duress raises a profound question: is it sincere? Historically, many people who were forced to abjure continued secretly holding their original beliefs. This is why courts and religious bodies demanded the abjuration be made publicly and under oath — they wanted to make backing out as difficult and shameful as possible.
How the word is used today

In modern English, "abjuration" lives mainly in formal, legal, historical, and literary writing. You will encounter it in historical accounts of religious persecution, in documents about renouncing citizenship or political allegiance, and in philosophical or literary writing where a weighty, decisive rejection is being described. It is not an everyday conversational word — when someone uses it, they are deliberately signalling that the rejection in question is not casual. It is grave, official, and final.

Here are a few example sentences to make the usage concrete:

"His abjuration of his former beliefs was read aloud before the entire congregation."
"The peace treaty required the abjuration of all territorial claims."
"Galileo's abjuration before the Inquisition remains one of history's most haunting moments of intellectual surrender."
"She filed a formal abjuration of her citizenship, closing the chapter on her previous life entirely."
The single sentence to remember it by

If you want one clean sentence to anchor this word in your memory: An abjuration is a formal, sworn, public act of completely and permanently rejecting something you once believed in or were loyal to — not a quiet change of heart, but an official declaration witnessed and recorded, carrying the full weight of an oath behind it.
83: To abjure something means to formally and solemnly declare that you are rejecting or giving it up — usually something you once believed in, were loyal to, or claimed as your own — and committing yourself to never returning to it. It is not merely stopping something or quietly changing your mind. It is making an official, binding break: deliberate, public, and meant to last.
What makes abjuring different from simply "giving up"

Three qualities give this word its precise meaning.

The first is formality. To abjure is to make a declared act, often before witnesses — in a courtroom, a religious setting, or some other official arena. It is not a private, internal decision you keep to yourself.

The second is solemnity. The act carries real weight and gravity. There is nothing flippant or offhand about it. The person doing it understands that this is serious.

The third is finality. You are not taking a break from something or pausing a belief — you are permanently renouncing it. This is meant to be a point of no return.

Together, these three qualities explain why "abjure" is a far stronger and weightier word than simply "quit," "drop," or "give up."
What kinds of things can be abjured

Abjure is used for things that carry real significance — things that once defined a person's convictions, loyalty, or identity. Religious beliefs or doctrines, political ideologies, allegiance to a leader or nation, a claim to power or a throne, and deeply held principles or ways of life are all things that can be abjured.

You would not ordinarily use this word for something trivial — like giving up sugar or skipping a habit. Though in rare, deliberately dramatic or poetic writing, you might see it applied to smaller things for rhetorical effect.
How it differs from similar words

Renounce is the closest synonym and can often be swapped in. But "abjure" leans more formal and ceremonial — it carries the sense of an oath being made, not just a personal choice.

Recant means specifically to withdraw something you previously stated or believed — a testimony, a position, a doctrine. It zeroes in on taking back what you said or claimed. "Abjure" can include this sense, but it is broader and carries a more binding, sworn quality.

Forswear is almost identical in spirit — both words involve seriously and solemnly swearing off something. In many contexts they are interchangeable. The difference is subtle and mostly one of tone.

Abandon simply means to leave or give up, without any ceremony, weight, or deliberateness. You can abandon something almost accidentally or gradually. Abjuring is always intentional and openly declared.

Reject is the most casual of the group — a quick, even internal dismissal. Abjuring always involves an outward, formal commitment.

Seeing the word in real sentences is the best way to lock in its meaning.

"Under pressure from the Inquisition, the scholar was forced to abjure his belief that the Earth moved around the Sun." — This is the most classic use of the word: a formal recantation made before an authority, under duress, of a previously held conviction. (This is a reference to what happened to Galileo.)

"After years of radicalism, he publicly abjured his extremist ideology and devoted himself to peaceful dialogue." — Here, abjuring marks a dramatic, declared turning point in a person's life. It signals a clean and permanent break.

"The rebel leader was given a choice: abjure his claim to the throne, or face imprisonment." — To abjure a claim means to formally and permanently surrender a right or entitlement you once asserted.

"During the naturalization ceremony, she abjured all loyalty to her former country and pledged allegiance to her new one." — This is a real-world example. Citizenship oaths in many countries include a formal renunciation of prior national loyalties, which is essentially an act of abjuring.

"He abjured alcohol entirely after the accident — not as a casual New Year's resolution, but as a solemn, public commitment." — Even for something personal like a habit, the word signals a weighty, binding decision rather than a simple lifestyle choice.
Where you are likely to encounter this word

"Abjure" is formal and is not used in everyday conversation. You will most often meet it in historical writing — particularly about medieval courts, religious tribunals, or political succession — in legal documents, in religious or philosophical texts dealing with heresy and conversion, in political writing about allegiance and ideology, and in literary fiction, especially historical novels.
To abjure something is to solemnly and formally swear it off — making a public, binding declaration that you are permanently rejecting something you once held, followed, or claimed.
84: The word ablaze essentially means intensely lit up — whether by real fire, by brilliant light and color, or by a powerful emotion burning inside a person. Think of it as a word that captures something burning or glowing with great intensity. The key feeling it always carries is "a lot, and powerfully so."

This is the most direct meaning. When something is ablaze, it is burning with fire — not just a small flicker, but actively and strongly burning.

Examples:

  • "The old warehouse was ablaze by midnight."
  • "Firefighters rushed to the scene as the forest was ablaze."

Note that "ablaze" feels more vivid and dramatic than simply saying "on fire." A journalist writing "the building was ablaze" paints a stronger, more intense picture than just saying "the building was on fire." This is why writers and reporters love this word — it carries weight and urgency.
Meaning 2: Brilliantly Bright with Light or Color 🌟

Here, nothing is actually burning. Instead, something is so bright, so colorful, or so vividly lit up that it looks like it's on fire. This is a figurative (imaginative) use of the word.

Examples:

  • "The autumn hillside was ablaze with red, orange, and yellow leaves."
  • "The concert hall was ablaze with thousands of tiny lights."
  • "The sky was ablaze at sunset."

In all these sentences, no fire exists. Instead, the colors or lights are so rich and intense that the word "ablaze" perfectly captures how overwhelming and vivid they look. You can close your eyes and feel how bright and striking the scene must be.

A person — or their eyes, face, or spirit — can be ablaze with a powerful emotion. This means they are overwhelmed by it, unable to contain it, as if it were a fire burning inside them.

Examples:

  • "Her eyes were ablaze with fury when she heard the news."
  • "The young activist spoke with a face ablaze with passion."
  • "He was ablaze with excitement on the morning of the championship."

The emotions most commonly paired with "ablaze" are strong ones: anger, passion, excitement, joy, determination. You wouldn't typically say someone was "ablaze with mild interest." The word demands intensity.
The Thread That Ties All Three Meanings Together

No matter which meaning you're looking at, ablaze always signals:intensity. Something ordinary is never described as "ablaze." The word is chosen specifically when something is a lot — burning a lot, glowing a lot, or feeling a lot.

This is what separates "ablaze" from weaker alternatives:

Instead of saying..."Ablaze" suggests...
"On fire"A powerful, dramatic fire
"Bright"Brilliantly, almost overwhelmingly bright
"Emotional"Burning with intense feeling
How "Ablaze" is Used in a Sentence (Grammar)

"Ablaze" is almost always placed after a verb, not directly before a noun. This is called a predicative adjective.

✅ "The forest was ablaze." (correct)
✅ "She set the paper ablaze." (correct)
✅ "His imagination ran ablaze." (correct)
❌ "An ablaze forest" — this sounds unnatural and is rarely used.

Also, notice the phrase "set ablaze" — it means to cause something to catch fire (literally or figuratively):

  • "The arsonist set the building ablaze."
  • "Her speech set the crowd ablaze with hope."
The Overall Feeling of the Word

"Ablaze" is a word with energy. It is not neutral or quiet. Whenever you read or hear it, it is a signal that something dramatic, vivid, and powerful is happening. A good way to test whether you truly understand a word is to ask: "What emotion does it create in me when I read it?" With "ablaze," the answer should be: a sense of brightness, heat, and power — something you cannot ignore or look away from.

That is the complete world of "ablaze."
85: When "ablaze" is used as an adverb, it modifies a verb — it tells you how something is burning, shining, or feeling. It means "in a fierce, blazing state" or "in a way that resembles a powerful fire." Think of a massive, roaring fire — uncontrolled, overwhelming, impossible to ignore. That image is the heart of the word. Whenever you see "ablaze," that picture of intense, consuming fire is always somewhere in the meaning, even when no actual fire is involved.

In its most straightforward sense, "ablaze" describes something burning fiercely and powerfully. It's not about a small flame or gentle burn. It is about a fire that is strong, fast, and wild.

  • "The old factory burned ablaze through the night, and smoke filled the sky for miles."

Here, "ablaze" tells you it wasn't smoldering — it was roaring with intense fire.

  • "The dry forest caught ablaze within seconds of the lightning strike."

It caught fire — suddenly and completely.

The word emphasizes that the fire is overwhelming, not just present. A candle flame is not "ablaze." A fully engulfed, raging bonfire is.
Meaning 2 — Glowing or Shining Very Brightly

"Ablaze" is also used to describe something that shines or glows with extreme brightness — so intensely that it looks as though it is "on fire" with light. No actual fire is involved here. It is purely about the visual intensity of the light.

  • "The city skyline glittered ablaze with thousands of lights reflected in the river."

The lights were so many and so bright that the skyline looked like it was burning.

  • "The autumn hillside blazed ablaze in shades of red, orange, and gold."

The colors were so vivid and rich that the hill looked like it was on fire.

  • "The stage lit up ablaze as the concert began."

The lights were overwhelmingly bright and dramatic — fire-like in their intensity.

This is a very visual use of the word. Writers and speakers use it when they want you to feel the brightness — not just imagine a dim glow, but a brilliance that hits your eyes like something burning.

This is perhaps the most common and powerful figurative use of "ablaze." It describes a person who is feeling an emotion so intensely that it seems like a fire burning inside them.

  • "She stared ablaze with fury when she discovered the betrayal."

Her anger was not mild irritation. It was fierce, burning, consuming — like fire.

  • "He spoke ablaze with passion, and the entire audience leaned in."

His passion was overwhelming, electric, impossible to ignore. His words carried the heat of genuine fire.

  • "Her eyes shone ablaze with determination as she crossed the finish line."

Her determination was fierce and bright — it radiated outward like a flame.

  • "The crowd cheered ablaze with excitement when the winning goal was scored."

The excitement was wild and uncontrollable — like a fire spreading through the stadium.

The emotions you'll most commonly see described with "ablaze" are: anger, passion, excitement, love, determination, enthusiasm, and desire — all strong, intense emotions that consume you. Quiet, gentle feelings are never described this way. You would not say someone smiled "ablaze with contentment." The emotion must feel like something on fire.
The One Thread Running Through All Three Meanings

Whether "ablaze" is describing an actual fire, a dazzling light, or an overwhelming emotion, one idea is always present: overwhelming intensity. Something ablaze is not moderate, calm, or contained. It is fully ignited — burning at full strength, nothing held back.

This is what separates "ablaze" from milder words. A small fire is not ablaze. A soft light is not ablaze. A quiet feeling is not ablaze. The word requires — and delivers — drama, scale, and force.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Aflame is nearly identical in meaning to "ablaze" and the two are often interchangeable. Both suggest fire and intensity. If anything, "ablaze" tends to feel slightly more dramatic and visual — conjuring a bigger, more consuming fire — while "aflame" can sometimes suggest a warmer, gentler burning.

Aglow shares the light/brightness meaning of "ablaze" but is much gentler. Something aglow has a soft, warm light — like a face lit by candlelight. Something ablaze has a fierce, overwhelming light — like a spotlight or a burning structure. "Aglow" is cozy; "ablaze" is intense.

Burning (as in "burning with anger") is close to the emotional meaning of "ablaze," but "ablaze" is more vivid and visual. "Burning with anger" is familiar and common. "Ablaze with anger" is more striking, more literary, more dramatic.
Register and Tone — When and Where You'll See This Word

"Ablaze" is not a word of everyday casual speech. You are unlikely to hear it in a normal conversation about ordinary things. It belongs to:

  • Literature and fiction — especially when a writer wants to paint a vivid, dramatic picture
  • Speeches and oratory — when a speaker wants to stir emotion
  • Journalism and news writing — especially headlines and dramatic descriptions of fires or events
  • Poetry — where intensity and imagery matter above all

When a writer reaches for "ablaze," they are making a deliberate choice. They want you to feel the heat, the brightness, the overwhelmingness. They are not reporting a fact neutrally — they are painting a picture that burns.

"Ablaze" as an adverb means "in an intensely burning, glowing, or passionate state." It modifies a verb to tell you that whatever is happening is happening with the fierceness and power of a blazing fire. It can describe:

  1. Actual fire — burning powerfully and out of control
  2. Light — shining with extreme, overwhelming brightness
  3. Emotion — feeling something with consuming, fire-like intensity

The one constant: everything ablaze is on full power — fierce, vivid, impossible to ignore, and far beyond ordinary.

Abligurition means extravagance, especially in matters of food and drink. More specifically, when you squander your money on treats and comfort foods, you are engaging in abligurition — excessive spending on food and drink.

Think of it this way: it's not just buying expensive food. It's recklessly spending money on food and drink, to the point where it becomes wasteful and financially irresponsible.
Breaking it down so the full picture is clear:

There are three core ideas packed into this one word:

  1. Spending — This is specifically about money, not appetite. It's not a word about eating too much (that's gluttony). It's about paying too much, too freely, too often, on food and drink.
  2. Excess — The spending isn't just generous or enthusiastic. It goes beyond what is reasonable or sensible. The word carries a clear sense of going too far.
  3. Food and drink specifically — This word doesn't apply to overspending in general (like buying too many shoes or too many cars). It is locked in on the domain of eating and drinking. It is a very targeted kind of financial recklessness.

Put all three together: abligurition is the act of wastefully throwing money at food and drink, beyond any reasonable limit.
The tone and feel of the word:

This is not a neutral word. It carries a negative judgment. When you describe someone's behavior as abligurition, you are implying they are being irresponsible — almost foolish — with their money in the pursuit of culinary pleasure. It suggests a lack of self-control where the wallet meets the dinner table.

It is close in spirit to words like "squandering" or "prodigal spending," both of which suggest waste and excess rather than simply enjoying fine things.

• Treating yourself to a nice meal occasionally → Not abligurition. A single splurge isn't the point.
  • Being a food lover or a "foodie" → Not abligurition. Appreciating great food is not the same as wastefully burning money on it.
  • Eating too much → Not abligurition. The word is about the money spent, not the quantity consumed.
  • Buying expensive food thoughtfully and within your means → Not abligurition. The recklessness and the "going overboard" quality are essential.
Scale: how extreme does it have to be?

It can apply to both a single grand act of excess or a pattern of behavior over time. A year of abligurition can drain a person's entire bank account. But it can also describe one spectacular, over-the-top event. Roman Emperor Vitellius once ate one thousand oysters in one day — a very impressive act of abligurition. Both cases qualify: what matters is that the spending is wildly disproportionate and indulgent.
In everyday language, you'd describe it as:
Burning through money on food and drink. Blowing your budget on feasts and drinks. Financially ruining yourself chasing culinary pleasures. The word wraps all of that into a single, precise term.

Very. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, this word is now considered obsolete, with its only recorded use in formal documentation dating to the early 1700s. It appears occasionally in literary writing for stylistic effect — to sound learned, colorful, or deliberately obscure. Its earliest documented use dates to 1724. So if you use it today, expect most people not to recognize it — which is part of its charm.
One sentence to remember it by:
Abligurition is what happens when a person's love of fine food and drink overrides their financial common sense — and they spend recklessly, even ruinously, at the table.
87: Ablution means the act of washing the body, particularly as a formal, ritual, or ceremonial act. Think of it as washing that carries a sense of purpose — not just rinsing your hands out of habit, but washing with intention, often as part of a religious or solemn routine.
The Two Main Worlds This Word Lives In

1. Religious and Ceremonial Use (Its Primary and Most Precise Use)

This is where the word truly belongs. Across many of the world's religions, washing certain parts of the body before worship or prayer is a sacred requirement. That act of ritual washing is called an ablution.

  • A Muslim washes their hands, face, arms, and feet before the five daily prayers. This is a classic example of ablution.
  • A Jewish worshipper ritually washes their hands before meals or prayer.
  • A Catholic priest washes his fingers during Mass.
  • A Hindu devotee bathes in a sacred river before worship.

In all these cases, the washing is not about dirt or hygiene in the everyday sense. It is about purification — cleansing oneself spiritually before approaching something holy. That is the soul of the word. The body is being washed, but the underlying intention is to become ritually clean or worthy.

2. Informal, Humorous, or Old-Fashioned Use

You will also sometimes see ablutions (almost always in the plural here) used to describe a person's ordinary daily washing — brushing teeth, washing the face, bathing, and so on.

For example: "He disappeared into the bathroom to perform his morning ablutions."

This usage is a little playful or old-fashioned. The speaker is borrowing the grand, ceremonial weight of the word and applying it to something mundane, which creates a slightly witty or formal effect. Think of it as someone describing their morning shower as if it were a sacred religious ritual — it's not wrong, but it has a tongue-in-cheek quality.
Singular vs. Plural — A Key Nuance

• Ablution (singular) tends to appear in formal, religious, or theological contexts, referring to the act or concept itself. "Ablution is required before prayer."
  • Ablutions (plural) is far more commonly seen and is the standard form in everyday writing, especially in the informal/humorous use. "She completed her ablutions and headed downstairs."
The Register of This Word (How Formal Is It?)

Ablution is a formal word. You would not drop it into casual conversation — it would sound odd and overly stiff. It belongs in:

  • Religious texts and discussions
  • Literary fiction, especially older or more elevated prose
  • Formal descriptions of ceremony or ritual
  • Occasionally, writing that deliberately uses it for effect or gentle humor

You would never say to a friend, "I just did my ablutions" in a normal, natural way. But you might write it in a story, or read it in a religious or historical text, and it would feel perfectly at home there.

• "Before entering the mosque, he performed his ablutions at the fountain outside." — Religious context, natural use.
  • "The priest's ablution of his hands is a moment of solemn preparation during the ceremony." — Ceremonial context.
  • "She took her time with her ablutions each morning, treating even a simple face-wash as a private ritual." — Informal/literary use.
  • "The monks rose before dawn, performed their ablutions in silence, and proceeded to prayer." — Formal, narrative use.
One Elegant Way to Remember It

Whenever you see the word ablution, picture a person standing at a basin or a river, washing themselves not out of necessity, but out of devotion or ceremony. The washing matters less as a physical act and more as a meaningful one. That sense of purposeful, respectful washing is the heartbeat of the word.

What it meansThe act of washing the body, especially as a ritual
Most important useReligious purification before prayer or worship
Secondary useA formal/humorous way to say "daily washing routine"
Typical form"Ablutions" (plural) in most everyday writing
ToneFormal, literary, ceremonial
88: To abnegate something means to deliberately and consciously give it up, reject it, or deny it — especially something of real importance or value. The key word is deliberately. This is always a chosen act, never an accident.
It works in two closely related ways:

1. To renounce or give up something external — such as a right, a responsibility, a belief, or a position of power.

A king who abnegates his throne is not being overthrown. He is choosing to walk away from royal power. A soldier who abnegates his duty is not simply failing — he is refusing to carry out what his role demands of him. A scientist who abnegates her earlier theories is formally and deliberately rejecting beliefs she once held.

2. To deny oneself — to suppress or sacrifice your own desires, needs, pleasures, or personal identity. This use is sometimes called "self-abnegation."

A monk who abnegates worldly pleasures chooses to live without comforts that most people enjoy — not because he has no access to them, but because he deliberately turns away from them. A devoted parent who abnegates their own needs for the sake of their children is consciously choosing to put themselves last.
The weight and feel of the word — this is where it gets precise:

Simply saying "give up" or "reject" doesn't quite capture what "abnegate" holds. The word carries three important layers that make it different from everyday alternatives:

It is always deliberate. Nobody abnegates something by accident. It is a conscious, intentional act.

It involves real sacrifice. You are not giving up something trivial. You are surrendering something of genuine value — a right, a belief, a pleasure, an identity, a role.

It carries gravity and principle. There is usually a moral, ethical, or deeply personal reason behind the act. A person who abnegates something is making a meaningful statement — not just a practical decision.

Here's a useful contrast: if someone gives up coffee for a week because they ran out, that is not abnegating. But if a monk chooses to permanently deny himself all physical comforts as a spiritual discipline, he is abnegating them. The difference is intention, weight, and principle.

It does not mean losing something against your will — that would be forfeiting or being stripped of something.

It does not mean the logical or mathematical sense of negating something (making it null or void).

It does not mean simply saying "no" to something in a casual, everyday way. Turning down a second slice of cake is not abnegating cake.
How it compares to similar words:

Renounce is the closest synonym — it also means to formally give something up. But "abnegate" carries a slightly heavier, more philosophical and self-sacrificing weight. You renounce a claim; you might abnegate your entire sense of personal desire or duty.

Relinquish means to let go of something, but without the same sense of principled rejection. You can relinquish a grip on something reluctantly and without any moral stance. Abnegate implies more conviction.

Forgo simply means to choose not to have something. It's lighter and carries no sense of sacrifice or solemn purpose. You might forgo dessert; you abnegate your worldly possessions.

Abdicate is specifically used when someone gives up a throne or formal position of power. Abnegate is broader — it can apply to rights, beliefs, desires, duties, and identity, not just positions of power.

Deny (oneself) is close to the self-abnegation meaning, but "abnegate" is more formal, more solemn, and suggests a deeper, more complete rejection.
Register — when and where you will see this word:

Abnegate is a formal, literary word. You will most often encounter it in serious essays, academic writing, philosophy, literature, and religious or moral discussions — particularly around themes of self-denial, duty, and sacrifice. You would rarely hear it in everyday conversation. Using it casually might sound deliberately dramatic or overly formal, which can be effective if that's your intention, but it is not a word of ordinary speech.
A simple anchor to remember it by:

Think of "abnegate" as the word for when someone makes a meaningful, deliberate choice to step away from something important to them — whether that's power, responsibility, pleasure, belief, or even their own sense of self. It is not casual walking away. It is a conscious, principled surrender.
89:
Abnegation means the act of giving something up or denying yourself something, usually deliberately and willingly. That "something" is typically a desire, a comfort, a pleasure, a right, or a personal interest.

Think of it this way: when a person steps back from what they want or what they could have, and chooses not to take it — that act of restraint and self-denial is abnegation.

This word carries two closely related meanings, and understanding both will give you complete mastery of it.

1. Self-denial for a higher purpose

This is the most common and important meaning. Abnegation is when a person willingly sacrifices their own needs, desires, or interests — usually out of duty, discipline, love, or a moral principle.

A monk who gives up material possessions and physical comfort to serve a spiritual life is practicing abnegation. A mother who gives up sleep, personal time, and her own ambitions to raise her children is practicing abnegation. A soldier who endures hardship and sets aside personal safety for the sake of the mission is practicing abnegation.

The key idea here is voluntariness — the person chooses to give something up. It is not taken from them. They surrender it themselves, and usually for something they consider more important than their own comfort or gain.

2. Renunciation of something (a right, a belief, a claim)

In a broader sense, abnegation also means the formal or deliberate giving up of a right, a position, a responsibility, or even a belief.

A king who gives up his throne is practicing abnegation of power. A person who publicly abandons a belief they once held strongly is practicing abnegation of that belief. This usage is slightly more formal and less common in everyday speech, but it belongs to the same family of meaning — the voluntary surrendering of something.
What Makes Abnegation Special (and Different from Similar Words)

You might be thinking: isn't this just sacrifice? Or self-control? Or abstinence? Here is how abnegation is distinct:

  • Sacrifice usually involves losing something painful in exchange for a specific outcome. You sacrifice your weekend to finish a project. Abnegation is broader — it is often an ongoing, principled practice of self-denial, not just a one-time trade-off.
  • Self-control is about resisting impulses in the moment. Abnegation goes deeper — it is a sustained and often conscious philosophy of putting your own wants aside.
  • Abstinence usually refers to avoiding a specific thing (food, alcohol, etc.). Abnegation is more general and carries a stronger moral or selfless tone.
  • Renunciation is perhaps the closest synonym, but abnegation tends to emphasize the personal cost and the selfless motive more strongly.

The word abnegation carries a tone of nobility and moral seriousness. When you use it, you are not just describing someone who skipped dessert. You are describing someone who, at real personal cost, chose discipline, duty, or the wellbeing of others over their own wants.

You will very often see abnegation paired with the word "self" — as in self-abnegation. This is simply an intensified or more explicit form of the same idea: the denial of oneself, one's own ego, desires, and interests. Some writers use "abnegation" and "self-abnegation" interchangeably. If anything, "self-abnegation" sometimes leans toward the idea of suppressing one's identity or ego, while "abnegation" alone can refer to giving up things in the world (rights, pleasures, power).

Mostly, but not always.

When used admiringly, abnegation describes a person of great discipline, selflessness, and moral strength. Saints, heroes, and devoted parents are described with this word in a positive light.

However, abnegation can also carry a slightly negative tone when the self-denial is seen as excessive, unhealthy, or unnecessary. If someone denies themselves every pleasure to the point of misery, or if they suppress their identity to please others out of fear, a writer might use "abnegation" critically — suggesting the person has gone too far and erased themselves in an unhealthy way.

So the word can cut both ways depending on the context, but the admiring, positive use is far more common.
How to Recognize It in a Sentence

Here are some constructed examples that show the word working naturally:

  • "The life of a great teacher often requires abnegation — placing the needs of students above personal ambition."
  • "His abnegation of wealth surprised everyone who knew how hard he had worked to earn it."
  • "She admired the abnegation of the volunteers, who worked long hours without pay or recognition."
  • "Years of abnegation and discipline had shaped him into a man of extraordinary focus."

In every case, notice the same thread: a person willingly setting aside something of personal value, driven by principle, love, duty, or a higher goal.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Abnegation is the deliberate, willing act of giving up your own desires, comforts, rights, or interests — usually driven by discipline, duty, selflessness, or a higher moral purpose.
